name: PCB design
title: From schematic to fab files
intro: Printed circuit boards turn schematics into copper. These lessons walk through schematic capture, footprints, layout rules, copper pours, design-rule checks, fabrication outputs and a look at assembly — enough to order a first prototype without guessing every acronym.

lessons.title: Schematic capture
lessons.summary: Drawing the circuit cleanly before layout.

sections.p: Schematic capture is drawing the circuit in EDA software (KiCad, Eagle, Altium…). Hierarchy, named nets and readable symbols prevent layout disasters. The schematic is the electrical contract; the PCB is the physical one.
Left-to-right signal flow, top power rails, bottom grounds when practical. Label important nets. Put decoupling capacitors next to their IC on the schematic so you remember them in layout.
Electrical rule checks catch undriven inputs, two outputs fighting, and missing power flags. Fix ERC before layout — copper will not heal a shorted net name.
Reference designators must be unique. Values must match what you will buy. A schematic that says 0.1 µF but a BOM that says 100 pF wastes a spin.

lessons.title: Footprints and land patterns
lessons.summary: The copper the part actually sits on.

sections.p: A footprint (land pattern) is the pads, courtyard and silk that match a physical part. The schematic symbol is logical; the footprint is geometric. Mismatches are a top cause of unusable boards.
Component datasheets recommend pad sizes. IPC guidelines refine them for density vs manufacturability. Measure a sample part if the library looks suspicious.
Courtyards keep parts from colliding. 3D models catch connector overhangs into enclosures before you order aluminium milled boxes.
Mark pin 1 in silk consistently. Polarised parts (diodes, electrolytics, connectors) need clear markings on both schematic and board.

lessons.title: Layout rules
lessons.summary: Clearance, width, and where parts sit.

sections.p: Layout places footprints and routes copper. Respect clearance (space between copper) and track width (current + fab limits). A 0.3 mm trace may be fine for signals; power paths need wider copper or pours.

Rough ballpark: a 1 mm trace on outer 1 oz copper carries on the order of a couple of amps with modest temperature rise — use a trace-width calculator for real designs. Vias add resistance; parallel vias help.
Every signal has a return. A solid ground plane under signal traces keeps loops small. Slots that force returns to detour create noise and EMI headaches.
Place connectors on edges, crystals close to MCU with short traces, decoupling caps tight to power pins. Think assembly and probing — can a human debug this?

sections.p: A copper pour (zone) fills an area with copper tied to a net — often GND or a power rail. Pours lower impedance, help heat spreading and simplify routing of returns.
Pads in a pour may use thermal relief spokes so hand soldering is possible. Solid connections sink heat into the plane and can make soldering harder.
Multi-layer boards stitch ground pours with vias so return currents can change layers. Around board edges, via fences sometimes help EMC — with thought, not superstition.
Unconnected copper islands can float and cause surprises — remove orphans or connect them deliberately. DRC/zone refill after edits.

lessons.title: Design rule checks
lessons.summary: Letting the computer find spacing mistakes.

sections.p: DRC (design rule check) compares your layout to constraints: clearance, track width, annular ring, hole size, courtyard overlap. Set rules to your fab's capabilities plus margin.
A cheap proto house might allow 0.15 mm clearance and 0.15 mm tracks. Tighter needs cost more. Do not design to the absolute minimum on a first board without reason.
DRC and connectivity checks find shorts between nets and unrouted ratsnest airwires. Clear every airwire before celebrating.
Silk on pads is a classic nuisance. Solder-mask expansion rules keep mask from covering pads. Run the checks your EDA offers for manufacturing layers too.

lessons.title: Fab files and BOM
lessons.summary: Gerbers, drill files and what to send.

sections.p: Fabricators need Gerber (or equivalent) layer plots, drill files, and usually a README noting layer stack, thickness and colour. Many shops also accept native KiCad/Eagle with caveats — Gerbers remain the lingua franca.
Typical two-layer set: top copper, bottom copper, top/bottom silk, top/bottom mask, board outline, drills. Four-layer adds inner planes. Name files clearly.
A BOM (bill of materials) lists every part to buy. For assembly services, a CPL/centroid file gives pick-and-place coordinates and rotations.
View Gerbers in a Gerber viewer before upload. Confirm outline, holes land on pads, and layers are not mirrored by mistake.

lessons.title: Assembly basics
lessons.summary: Hand stuff, stencil paste and order of operations.

sections.p: Assembly puts parts on the fabricated board. Hobbyists hand-solder; services use solder paste stencils, pick-and-place, and reflow ovens. Design choices (fiducials, spacing) affect how easy assembly is.
Often: low parts first, then taller. Or all SMD reflow first, then through-hole. Polarised parts get double-checked before heat.
A stainless stencil aligns to pads; paste is squeegeed through apertures. Paste volume depends on aperture design — another reason footprints matter.
Check bridges, tombstoned passives, polarity marks and missing parts. Power up with current limit on a first article. Smoke is a teacher; prefer not to summon it.
Small boards may be panelised with mouse bites or V-grooves. Add fiducials for machines. Ask the assembler what they need.

lessons.title: Layers and stackup
lessons.summary: Two-layer vs four-layer and what changes.

sections.p: Stackup is how copper and insulating layers are ordered. A two-layer board has top and bottom copper. A four-layer board often puts signals on outside layers and continuous ground/power planes inside — quieter and easier for dense designs.

Tight routing, fast edges, or picky analog sections benefit from planes. Cost is higher than two-layer but prototypes are still affordable. Controlled impedance needs specified stackup dielectric thickness.
USB, HDMI and RF traces may need 50 Ω or 90 Ω differential controlled impedance. That is a conversation with the fab's stackup chart — not a guess at track width alone.
Many first projects succeed on two-layer with a poured ground bottom and careful routing on top. Master that before chasing exotic RF stackups.
